title: Lease
explain: A lease is ownership that expires on its own. The holder keeps it only by renewing, so if it crashes the ownership frees itself and someone else can take over — nobody has to detect the failure. It is like a hotel key card that stops working at checkout without you handing it back.
model:
`Lease(resource, owner, expires_at)` issued by one **lease authority**.

```
grant ──▶ renew ──▶ renew ──▶ (stop renewing) ──▶ expire ──▶ grant to someone else
```

- **Renew interval < TTL**, typically TTL ≈ 3 × interval, so one lost renewal is survivable.
- **Liveness, not safety.** Expiry guarantees the resource is never stuck; it does not stop a paused holder from acting late. Pair it with a [fencing token](#/sd/f/fencing-token).
- **Who grants leases?** Only the single owner of the state machine (the orchestrator). A dispatcher, gateway or message queue passes work along but never owns the lease.

details.q: Why use a lease instead of a lock that the holder releases?
details.a: A released lock depends on the holder being alive to release it; a crashed holder would hold it forever unless something detects the crash. A lease needs no detection: time does the release.

details.q: How long should the lease be?
details.a: Long enough to ride out a GC pause or a network blip (renew every TTL/3), short enough that failover — up to one full TTL after the last renewal — is acceptable. It is the failover-time vs false-takeover trade-off.

details.q: What happens if the holder pauses past its expiry and then keeps working?
details.a: It may act on a resource someone else now owns. The lease alone cannot stop that; the resource must reject stale holders with a fencing token.
The lease authority's. Holders should stop working a margin *before* their local view of expiry, and the authority should wait a margin *after*, to absorb clock skew.

details.q: Why must only the orchestrator own leases?
details.a: The lease is part of the state machine (who is working on what). If a middle layer like a queue or dispatcher also tracks ownership, there are two sources of truth and they will disagree after a failure.

prompts.q: Explain a lease to an interviewer, with an analogy, in under 30 seconds.
points: A crash frees it without failure detection

prompts.q: A worker holding a job lease crashes. Walk through what happens, and how long until the job runs again.
points: The lease expires up to one TTL after the last renewal
The authority grants it to another worker
Failover time is bounded by the TTL

prompts.q: Say what a lease does and does not guarantee, and what you add to cover the gap.
points: Liveness: the resource is never stuck
Not safety: a paused holder can act late
Add a fencing token checked by the resource
